# AI Alignment: A Contemporary Survey

Authors: Jiaming Ji, Tianyi Qiu, Boyuan Chen, Jiayi Zhou, + 25, Borong Zhang, Donghai Hong, + 23, Hantao Lou, Kaile Wang, Yawen Duan, Zhonghao He, + 19, Lukas Vierling, Zhaowei Zhang, Fanzhi Zeng, Juntao Dai, Xuehai Pan, Hua Xu, Aidan O'Gara, Kwan Ng, Brian Tse, Jie Fu, Stephen Mcaleer, Yanfeng Wang, Mingchuan Yang, Yunhuai Liu, Yizhou Wang, Song-Chun Zhu, Yike Guo, Yaodong Yang, Wen Gao (Less) Authors Info & Claims

Published: 21 November 2025 Publication History

## Abstract

### Abstract

AI alignment aims to make AI systems behave in line with human intentions and values. As AI systems grow more capable, so do risks from misalignment. To provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of the alignment field, in this survey, we delve into the core concepts, methodology, and practice of alignment. First, we identify four principles as the key objectives of AI alignment: Robustness, Interpretability, Controllability, and Ethicality (RICE). Guided by these four principles, we outline the landscape of current alignment research and decompose them into two key components: forward alignment and backward alignment. The former aims to make AI systems aligned via alignment training, while the latter aims to gain evidence about the systems’ alignment and govern them appropriately to avoid exacerbating misalignment risks. On forward alignment, we discuss techniques for learning from feedback and learning under the distribution shift. Specifically, we survey traditional preference modeling methods and reinforcement learning from human feedback and further discuss potential frameworks to reach scalable oversight for tasks where effective human oversight is hard to obtain. Within learning under distribution shift, we also cover data distribution interventions such as adversarial training that helps expand the distribution of training data and algorithmic interventions to combat goal misgeneralization. On backward alignment, we discuss assurance techniques and governance practices. Specifically, we survey assurance methods of AI systems throughout their lifecycle, covering safety evaluation, interpretability, and human value compliance. We discuss current and prospective governance practices adopted by governments, industry actors, and other third parties, aimed at managing existing and future AI risks. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive yet beginner-friendly review of alignment research topics. Based on this, we also release and continually update the website www.alignmentsurvey.com which features tutorials, collections of papers, blog posts, and other resources.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advancements have seen the increasing application of capable AI systems in complex domains. For instance, Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited improved capabilities in multi-step reasoning [207] and cross-task generalization [30] in real-world deployment settings, and these abilities are strengthened with increased training time, data, and parameter size [13, 146]. The utilization of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for the control of nuclear fusion [57] is another notable example. The increasing capabilities and deployment in high-stakes domains come with heightened risks. Various undesirable behaviors exhibited by advanced AI systems (e.g., manipulation [177] and deception [94]) have raised concerns about the hazards from AI systems.

These concerns have heightened research interest in AI alignment [87]. AI alignment aims to make AI systems behave in line with human intentions and values, focusing more on the objectives of AI systems than their capabilities. Efforts in AI alignment are directed at addressing system failures, characterized by deviations from human intentions and the manifestation of undesirable behaviors, through the pursuit of four key objectives (Section 1.3.2): Robustness, Interpretability, Controllability, and Ethicality (RICE). Current research and practice on alignment consist of four areas (Section 1.3): Learning from Feedback (Section 2), Learning under Distributional Shift (Section 3), Assurance (Section 4), and Governance (Section 5). The four areas and the RICE objectives are not in one-to-one correspondence. Each individual area often serves more than one alignment objective, and vice versa (see Table 1). In this survey, we review the concept, methodology, and practice of AI alignment and discuss its future directions.

### 1.1 The Concept of Alignment: A History of Ideation

The concept of AI alignment originates from thought experiments like the “paperclip maximizer” [24], which illustrates how a powerful AI, if given a misspecified objective, could pursue it to catastrophic ends. This highlights the risk of instrumental convergence [145], where intelligent agents are likely to pursue common sub-goals like self-preservation and resource acquisition, potentially overriding human control. The concern is that economic incentives and competitive pressures might lead to the deployment of such powerful systems recklessly [140]. In response, various conceptual frameworks have been developed to address these alignment challenges.

Agent Foundations. Early research, finding standard reinforcement learning (RL) formalisms insufficient for ensuring the safety of powerful AI, spurred the development of agent foundations [180]. This area explores alternative models to address fundamental issues. One key problem is the failure of standard RL to handle out-of-distribution scenarios; the AIXI framework [121] offers a non-parametric Bayesian approach as a potential solution. Another challenge is enabling an agent to reason about its own potential for self-modification, which requires models where the agent is part of the environment, raising issues of self-reference that have been addressed through theoretical constraints and causal modeling [115]. A final example is managing the complexity of human values, which are difficult to specify as a simple reward function. This has led to models where utility is represented as a collection of negotiated “shards” or sub-agents [158].

Game-theoretic Conceptualizations. To better capture the interactive nature of alignment, game-theoretic models treat humans as agents within the system, not just as external sources of reward. The off-switch game [83] formalizes the incentive for an AI to prevent its shutdown. The assistance game framework [84] models the AI’s task as inferring and acting upon a human’s unknown objectives. The cooperative inverse reinforcement learning (CIRL) [174], which will be detailed in Section 2, enables human guidance to AI to jointly maximize the ground truth reward, also falls under the category of such methods. However, significant open problems remain, including the inherent difficulty of accurately inferring human preferences from behavior and the challenge of accounting for changing or influenceable human values [11].

Systemic Conceptualizations. Since real-world AI deployment involves complex systems, recent frameworks analyze alignment from a broader, systemic perspective. One approach argues that safety should be a property of a deployment protocol rather than the AI itself, leading to the evaluation of control mechanisms that tradeoff utility and reliability [79]. Another effort focuses on building guaranteed safe AI (GSAI) by formally verifying that an AI’s actions adhere to safety specifications, drawing on methodologies from established safety-critical fields [53]. Finally, scholars are considering the wide-ranging societal externalities of AI. This has led to expanded conceptualizations of alignment’s goals, moving from a single human-AI pair to collective delegation [47]. The aims have been redefined in various ways, such as achieving “appropriateness” to social context [120], human “empowerment” [62], or fostering “collective truth-seeking” [49, 114], while considering the risks of gradual disempowerment at a societal scale [88].

### 1.2 The Contemporary Motivation for Alignment

The contemporary motivation for alignment is a three-step argument, each step building upon the previous one: (1) Deep learning-based systems have an increasingly large impact on society and bring significant risks; (2) Misalignment represents a significant source of risks; and (3) Alignment research and practice address risks stemming from misaligned systems. In this section, we discuss the risks associated with misalignment and the causes that drive them.

The scope of the article, especially when it comes to alignment methods, intersects with multiple branches of machine learning. However, a large part of the terminology in this section will be taken from the RL branch. This is because many of the most salient failure modes explained in this section emerge during RL training, as RL explicitly trains the model to be goal-driven—a property that both enables agency and causes hazard [140].

#### 1.2.1 Risks of Misalignment.

With improved capabilities of AI systems, come increased risks. Some undesirable behaviors of LLMs including untruthful answers, sycophancy [177], and deception [94] worsen with increased model scale, resulting in concerns about advanced AI systems that are hard to control. Moreover, emerging trends such as LLM-based agents [130] also raise concerns about the system’s controllability and ethicality [183, 189, 216]. Looking further ahead, the development of increasingly competent AI systems opens up the possibility of realizing Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in the foreseeable future, i.e., systems that can match or surpass human intelligence in all relevant aspects [171]. This could bring extensive opportunities [133], but also come with serious risks.

Within the large-scale risks from superhuman capabilities, it has been conjectured that global catastrophic risks (i.e., risks of severe harms on a global scale) [25] and existential risks (i.e., risks that threaten the destruction of humanity’s long-term potential) from advanced AI systems are especially worrying. These concerns are elaborated in first-principle deductive arguments [88], evolutionary analysis [86], and scenario mapping. Existential risks from AI also include risks of value lock-in and more [88], in addition to extinction risks. Governments and civil society have called for the prevention of, and taken a range of measures to address, such risks [191].

#### 1.2.2 Causes of Misalignment.

The previous section discussed the alignment motivation in terms of AI risks and the ethics of technology. We now examine why and how misalignment issues arise.

Overview of Failure Modes. To illustrate the misalignment issue, we give an overview of alignment failure modes, most of which can be categorized into reward hacking and goal misgeneralization.

Reward Hacking. Proxy rewards are often easy to optimize but fail to capture the full scope of true rewards, a limitation known as misspecified rewards. Optimizing for such misspecified rewards leads
